catalog_quote: As in many Indian languages, the stress-accent of any particular word in Takelma is not so inseparably associated with any particular syllable but that the same word, especially if consisting of more than two syllables, may appear with the main stress-accent now on one, now on the other syllable. In the uninterrupted flow of the sentence it becomes often difficult to decide which syllable of a word should be assigned the stress-accent. ... readall_conflicts: No disagreement among what was opened for this item, because the single listed work (Golla 2011) yielded nothing: the copy we hold is front matter only. One labelling tension worth noting for the catalog: the catalog records Takelma as 'tonal' with an empty rule, whereas the primary description already held by the project in our files (Sapir 1922 / Collected Works VIII, §5 'Stress and pitch accent', BAE Bull. 40 pp. 15-16 = CW VIII pp. 31-32; downloaded 2026-09-16 by an earlier reading, NOT a listed work here) describes a mobile stress-accent -- "the stress-accent of any particular word in Takelma is not so inseparably associated with any particular syllable but that the same word, especially if consisting of more than two syllables, may appear with the main stress-accent now on one, now on the other syllable" -- whose stressed syllable "takes on one of two or three musical inflections" (raised, rising, falling pitch). That is a stress-plus-pitch accent system rather than lexical tone in the usual sense, so 'tonal' with no stress statement undersells it; Golla's §4.3 title 'Pitch Accent and Tone' (p. 209) suggests he treats it under the same heading, but the page itself was not available to check.

audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: The classification (tonal / pitch accent, no positional stress rule, accent placement lexical-grammatical with minimal pairs by place of accent and by pitch contour) rests on Sapir's 296-page reference grammar, the only first-hand description of this extinct isolate, and every quoted passage and locator was confirmed in the full text we hold (pp. 15-16, 20, 55, 283). Glottolog's descriptive bibliography contains nothing on Takelma phonology beyond Sapir and its 1990 reprint, which I downloaded (open archive.org text) and which confirms the passages and documents that no later fieldwork exists. The one refinement available in the literature is Sapir's own 1936 phonemicization (reported in the downloaded volume via Hymes/Shipley, and presumably in Golla 2011): the raised and rising 'inflections' are length-conditioned variants, leaving a two-way pitch contrast on a freely placed accent. sources.quote: Photographic reprint of the 1912 grammar: same sec. 5 text ('As in many Indian languages, the stress-accent ...', three musical inflections, pitch-only minimal pairs). Golla's introduction adds that the description rests on 1.5 months with a single Lower Takelma speaker in 1906 and that no significant later work on the language exists beyond Harrington 1933; it offers no reanalysis of the accent.

sources.quote: Texts key: falling accent = fall in pitch of stressed vowel; raised accent 'found on short vowels or unitonal long vowels ... It is best considered as abbreviated form of' the rising accent; rising accent 'found only on long vowels and diphthongs'. Hymes note 1: the retranscription 'follows a phonemicization proposed by Sapir in lectures to his students at Yale in 1936' (tabulated in Shipley 1969:227, via Haas), in which 'pitch accent marking now follows the usual pattern of acute accent for high and grave for low'.
